newsitem.title: USA: USDA data shows more cattle on feed than expected.
newsitem.headline: USDA data shows more cattle on feed than expected.

text.p: Lower feed costs and improving profits enticed cattle feeders to put four percent more cattle in feedyards during September than a year ago, as borne out by Friday's U.S. Agriculture Department Cattle on Feed Report, analysts said.
The resulting larger fed cattle supply is seen weighing on Chicago Mercantile Exchange live cattle futures Monday.
"Feedlots have been making some pretty decent money and its not a surprise that they are replacing cattle," said Dave Maher, senior livestock analyst for Securities Corp of Iowa.

September cattle placements at major feedlots with 1,000 head or more capacity came in at 104 percent of a year ago on the report -- the high end of pre-report estimates which ranged from 96 to 104 percent and well above the 98.6 average.

September marketings tallied 84 percent of a year ago, the low end of the 85-95 percent range of estimates. This was also seen bearish for futures as it added to the number of cattle on feed which was put at 97 percent of last year, the high end of pre-report estimates which ranged from 93 to 97 percent.
"I think this report is certainly going to put the market on the defensive," said Don Close, analyst for Pioneer Hi-Bred.
Close also noted that grain prices were dropping at a rate that provided markedly improved opportunities to feed cattle.
Early trader and analyst expectations on Monday's CME live cattle opening were mostly 0.500 to 0.750 cent per lb lower due to the report.

However, a CME panel of market experts later Friday tempered their call on the futures opening to 0.400 to 0.500 cent lower, citing the already-large discount of the December contract to current cash levels and other factors.

"Our (December) discount to October futures is at a record level - I do believe we did price in a lot of negativness of the (report) figures," said panelist James Rose, floor broker for Iowa Grain Co.

CME October cattle futures ended Friday before the release of the report at 71.925 cents a lb compared with December futures at 65.350 cents. Also, cash cattle sold in direct sales at Plains area feedyards this week at $70.00 per cwt.
Rose also said that slaughter cattle weights indicated feedlots were current in their marketings coming into October.

Panelist Andy Gottschalk, senior vice president of LFG, agreed, noting slaughter cattle are running 10 lbs below year ago levels and show marketings are current and the feedlot industry in very good shape, he said. These factors could lend support to cash markets and futures.
USDA estimated the average of slaughter cattle weights the week ended October 5 at 1,185 lbs, down a lb from 1,186 the previous week and down nine lbs from 1,194 a year earlier.

"If we look at a normal marketing rate throughout the balance of the year, front end supplies project to remain well below year ago levels right through the end of the year and right into the first quarter of next year," Gottschalk said.
"I believe there is a good opportunity that this market can remain above $67 on a cash basis through the balance of this year, given the very current posture the fed cattle industry is in," he added.
